projectDesc.p: The digital part of the SNSF project 'Caroline Spurgeon: Chaucer Allusions, Shakespeare's Imagery, and the Digital Humanities' aims to create the first open-access database dedicated to the criticism and reception of Chaucer throughout history. It draws on the compilation and cataloguing work carried out by Professor Caroline Spurgeon (1869–1942) and collected in 'Five Hundred Years of Chaucer Criticism and Allusion'. This work consists of three volumes and a supplement, which will be systematically transcribed, corrected, enriched, encoded and published online, in order to facilitate future research and bring new perspectives to light.

editorialDecl.p: The original spelling and punctuation are retained. Meaningful layouts are reproduced, i.e. verses, printed marginalia, dots lines, tables, etc. However, we do not consider, the line breaks for prose, the columns or the curly brackets. The same rules apply for special characters and glyphs. Otiose letters are normalised, as well as spaces before punctuation marks.

div.ab: 1895. Unknown. Review (No. III) of The Complete Works of Geoffrey Chaucer, edited... by Walter W. Skeat, Oxford, vols. iv-vi, [in] The Nation, New York, vol. Ix, March 28, 1895, pp, 239-40.

ab.seg: [A critical review of the essay on sources of the tales (vol. iii) stating, that though the discussion is in the main satisfactory, "still, there are conspicuous inequalities, some unaccountable omissions, and a few errors." The reasoning as to the date of the 'Man of Law's Tale' is not very close; the existence of a verse translation of Innocent's 'De Con¬ temptu Mundi' is confidently asserted on very weak grounds; in the matter of Ser Giovanni and Il Pecorone Skeat seems to have disregarded recent Italian research; the vexed question of Chaucer's relations to Gower is left in an unsatisfactory condition; a serious mistake is the ascription of the 'Roman de la Manekine' and Philippe de Reimes; the summary of the literature of the 'Prioress's Tale' is meagre and out of date; more could have been made of the notes on the 'Wife of Bath's Tale.' The text of the 'Canterbury Tales' (vol. iv) is admirable, accurate and readable. The notes to the 'C. Tales' suffer from two general faults: (1) an attempt to serve the tyro and the adept; (2) discursiveness and lack of condensation. being "the very worst note ever written on a passage of Skeat's notes on the Prioress's French is condemned as Chaucer, as some of Mr. Skeat's come near being the very best." Yet in Chaucer annotation Skeat "has accomplished enough to justify one in associating his name with that of Tyrwhitt, and no Chaucerian can ask for higher honor." The general Introduction (vol. vi) affords a number of new observations, especially on metre, and the glossary is admirable. The Reviewer concludes that Skeat "may rest secure of the gratitude of more than one generation."]
